cenas.sub: What it is and how to read the chart

cenas.texto: The crossover gives the signal. The trend gives the direction.
cenas.fala: Hi, I'm Ricardo Garcia, and this is the TrendShot Bootcamp from MoreThanMoney. It's two videos. In this first one we'll understand what TrendShot is and how to read each element of the chart. TrendShot is a trend-following scalping system. It always enters in the direction the market is already moving, and it works mainly on the one-minute and five-minute charts. Before we start, one idea that runs through everything: the signal is the trigger, but it is not the decision. The decision depends on confirmations that you'll learn to validate. Let's take it one piece at a time.

itens: Video 1 · The system and each element of the chart
Video 2 · Signal, confirmations, management and routine
cenas.fala: The bootcamp has two videos. In the first, you'll understand the system, the markets it works on, and what each element on the chart means: the crossover triangle, the background histogram, the stars, the automatic structure, the 238 average, the POC and the volume. In the second, we get into the decision: the four confirmations, the entry, the stop, the target, managing the trade when a reversal star appears, when not to enter, and a routine for your session. Watch the videos in order. Each one builds on the one before.

cenas.sub: Scalping in the direction of the trend
cenas.fala: Chapter one: so what exactly is TrendShot?

itens: Always enters in the direction the market is already moving
The guide calls it pip surfing: riding the move
Trades last minutes, at most a few hours
Assets: indices like the US30, gold, BTC and forex pairs
cenas.fala: TrendShot is a scalping system that follows the trend. The idea is simple to say and takes discipline to carry out: you always enter in the direction the market is already moving. The guide calls it pip surfing, a way of riding the move while it lasts. Trades last minutes, at most a few hours. It isn't a system for holding a trade for days. As for assets, the guide points to indices like the US30, gold, on the XAUUSD pair, BTC and forex pairs. The system is the same across all of them. Each market behaves differently, and you'll learn that through practice on a demo account.

itens: A demo account with your broker
Access to TrendShot by MTM, through MoreThanMoney
One-minute and five-minute charts
A notebook or sheet for your journal
Time to be present during sessions
cenas.fala: Before we go on, here's what you need. A demo account with your broker, because everything you learn should be practised without real money first. Access to TrendShot by MTM, through MoreThanMoney. One-minute and five-minute charts, because that's where the system works. A notebook or a sheet for your journal. And time to be present during sessions, because a scalping system doesn't work well when you only glance at it. If you can't be present, TrendShot may not be your style, and that's an honest choice.

cenas.titulo: Reading the chart, piece by piece
cenas.fala: Chapter two: how to read the chart, piece by piece.

This is the chart with everything on, for a buy. One note I'll make just once in this bootcamp: the charts you see are illustrative. They're there to explain the reading. They are not real results or market history. Now, what you can see. The two exponential averages, the red twenty and the blue fifty, which cross to give the signal. The coloured background, which shows the direction. The horizontal lines, which are the automatic support and resistance structure. The dotted gold line, which is the POC. And the triangle, which marks the crossover. The plan lines appear afterwards. We'll go through each element on its own, because each one answers a different question.

itens: Red 20 average crosses above blue 50: blue triangle, buy
Crosses below: red triangle, sell
Each switch marks a short change of direction
The crossover is the trigger, not the decision
cenas.fala: The signal comes from the crossing of two exponential averages. The red one, at twenty, and the blue one, at fifty. When the red crosses above the blue, a blue triangle appears: that's a buy signal. When it crosses below, a red triangle appears: that's a sell signal. Each switch marks a short change of direction, which is why the system works in minutes. But notice a line from the guide worth keeping: the crossover is the trigger, not the decision. The triangle tells you something has changed. It doesn't tell you to enter. The decision only exists after the confirmations, and those are what we'll learn in the second video.

The background histogram shows the direction. It's blue while the 20 average sits above the 50, which is an uptrend. When the 20 drops below the 50, the background turns red, which is a downtrend. With a blue background you look for buys. With a red background you look for sells. The guide asks you to hold the trade while the colour doesn't change. Here, the colour is your patience gauge. When the background changes colour, the underlying direction has changed, and that matters far more than a single candle's move. Notice that this chart is a sell, with a red background and the averages in the downtrend position.

cenas.sub: Reversal warnings and where price stalls
cenas.fala: Chapter three: the stars and the automatic structure.

cenas.titulo: Warnings that move with the price
itens: Yellow: a small pullback
Blue: a deeper pullback, without changing the trend
Red in an uptrend, green in a downtrend: a possible turn
If price moves above a star, it wants to continue
cenas.fala: The stars are reversal warnings. They move with the price until they settle. A yellow star points to a small pullback. A blue one points to a deeper pullback, but one that doesn't change the trend. And a red star, in an uptrend, or a green one, in a downtrend, points to a possible turn in the trend. There's a simple reading rule: if the price moves through a star, it's because it wants to continue in that direction. The star is a warning about the move, not an order. Later you'll see that the guide treats it as an order to protect, not an order to exit. That difference matters.

On this chart, the red star marks the top of the rise. After it comes a sell. When the move down reaches a bottom, a green star appears, and a new rise begins. Notice that the stars aren't signals on their own. They're context, and they appear at moments when the move may be running out of steam. If you're long and a large red star appears, that's a warning to protect. If you're short and a green one appears, it's the same. The guide is clear about that, and the second video shows exactly how that protection is managed.

itens: Green lines above the price are resistances
Red lines below the price are supports
Breakout: the line turns red and becomes support
The retest is often where averages and structure work together
cenas.fala: The market structure is drawn automatically. Green lines above the price are resistances, and red lines below it are supports. When the price breaks a resistance, the line turns red and starts working as a support. The retest of that line is often a place where the averages and the structure work together. This helps you see where the price may stall, and where it may find support. It isn't a guarantee that it stalls, but it's one of the pieces that tells you whether the path to the target is clear or whether there are obstacles ahead.

cenas.sub: What the corner of the chart tells you
cenas.fala: Chapter four: the trend table, the 238 average, the POC and the volume.

itens: Trend table: the direction across several timeframes
Orange line: the 238 average
Dotted gold line: the POC, the level with the most volume
Corner of the chart: Good Volume or Low Volume
cenas.fala: The trend table shows the direction across several timeframes at once. The orange line is the 238 average. On the one-minute chart, it matches the fifty average of the five-minute chart. It's your longer context. The dotted gold line is the POC, the level with the most volume traded. And the corner shows Good Volume or Low Volume. The guide says the system performs better with liquidity and fast moves. With Low Volume, trading isn't forbidden, but the moves tend to be shorter. Notice that these pieces don't give you a signal. They give you context, and that context is what you'll use in the confirmations.

itens: 20/50 crossover: the trigger
Background histogram: the direction
Stars: reversal and protection warnings
Structure, 238 average and POC: the context
No single piece decides on its own
cenas.fala: Let's put the pieces together, so you can see each one's job. The 20/50 crossover is the trigger: it tells you the minute-scale move has changed. The background histogram is the direction: it tells you which side you're on. The stars are reversal warnings, and they ask you to protect the trade when you're on the wrong side of a star. The automatic structure, the 238 average and the POC are the context: they tell you where the price may stall, and whether there's room to the target. No single piece decides on its own. A triangle with the background against it, or with the 238 average on the wrong side, isn't an entry. It's just a triangle. The system only makes sense when the pieces are read together.

Look at this example. The arrows alternate from one side to the other, the histogram changes colour several times, and the averages are tangled. This is consolidation. The guide is clear: these signals are not taken. There's no wave to catch. And notice the corner: Low Volume. Many people get in here because the chart seems to be giving signals all the time, and that's exactly the mistake. A triangle in a market without direction is just another mark on the screen. Stay out, and let the next crossover with a clear direction be your target.

itens: Treating every yellow star as an exit
Entering a zone of tangled averages
Reading only one timeframe and ignoring the table
Confusing a protection star with an exit order
cenas.fala: Before we close this video, the most common reading mistakes. First, treating every yellow star as an exit. The guide says they appear often and tend to be only pullbacks. Second, entering a zone of tangled averages, where signals alternate from one side to the other. Third, reading only one timeframe and ignoring the trend table. And fourth, confusing a protection star with an exit order. A reversal star asks you to protect the trade. It doesn't tell you to leave. Write these mistakes in your journal when you see them, because they're the ones that cost the most to people who are learning.

itens: The four confirmations, in order
Entry on the crossover triangle
Stop on the other side of the two averages
Target at 1:2, and managing the stars
When not to enter, and the routine
cenas.fala: Welcome to the second video of the TrendShot Bootcamp. In the first you learned to read the chart. Now we move on to the decision. We'll go through the four confirmations, in order, and only then the entry on the crossover triangle. Then the stop, on the other side of the two averages, and the target, which the guide sets at at least double the stop. We'll also look at how to manage the trade when a reversal star appears, when not to enter, and a simple routine for your session. The system is fast. Your preparation has to be even calmer.

cenas.sub: If any one fails, let it go
cenas.fala: Chapter one: the four confirmations.

itens: Trend on two timeframes above
238 average behind the price
POC behind the price, or room to it
Good Volume
cenas.fala: Before you accept a signal, pass four confirmations. The first is the trend. Look at the two timeframes above yours, and want the same direction on all three. The second is the 238 average. On a buy, the orange line has to be below the price. On a sell, above it. The third is the POC. On a buy, it has to be below the price. On a sell, above. If it isn't behind you yet, confirm there's enough room before it, and factor it into the target. The fourth is Good Volume. The guide says the system performs better with liquidity and fast moves. And here's the final rule: if any one of these confirmations fails, let it go. A weak signal you missed costs nothing.

Let's apply the four confirmations to a buy. The blue triangle marks the red twenty crossing above the fifty. The background is blue, and the table shows the same direction on the two timeframes above. The 238 average, the orange line, is below the price. The POC, the dotted gold line, is also below. And the corner shows Good Volume. Four out of four. Notice something: the confirmations don't guarantee the move continues. They tell you the context is on your side right now. The decision to enter is still a step you take with the plan and the risk already calculated.

cenas.titulo: How to check the higher trend
itens: On the one-minute chart, check the five and the fifteen
On the five-minute chart, check the fifteen and the thirty
The same direction on all three; the table shows it at once
Different directions in the table: let it go
cenas.fala: The first confirmation deserves a detail. On the one-minute chart, you check the five and the fifteen. On the five-minute chart, you check the fifteen and the thirty. You want the same direction on all three. The trend table shows this at once, so you don't have to switch charts to check. If the table shows different directions on the timeframes above, let it go. You'd be trying to make a minute-scale move against an hour-scale trend, and the system doesn't recommend that fight. The larger context leads, and the small signal has to agree with it.
Chapter two: entry, stop and target.

linhas: on the other side of the two averages
stop of 25 pips, target of 50 pips
cenas.fala: There are three levels, plus an example from the guide. The entry is on the crossover triangle, once you've passed the confirmations. The stop sits on the other side of the two averages, the red and the blue. Notice it isn't a fixed distance. It's where the reading of the crossover stops making sense. The target is at least double the stop, which means a risk of one to two. The guide's example is a stop of twenty-five pips and a target of fifty. The POC and the earlier large stars help you refine the target. And before you send the order, calculate the position size using the risk you've decided on. The system draws the plan, but you define the lot size.

itens: Read the direction: histogram colour and table
Wait for the 20/50 crossover triangle
Check there are no stars or resistances ahead
Pass all four confirmations
Stop, 1:2 target and size, then the order
cenas.fala: Let's put the sequence in order. One: read the direction, using the histogram colour and the trend table. Two: wait for the 20/50 crossover triangle. Three: confirm there are no stars or resistances blocking the path just ahead. Four: pass all four confirmations, and only enter if every one is met. Five: set the stop on the other side of the two averages, the target at at least double the distance, and the position size. Only then does the order go to your broker. If any step fails, the trade doesn't exist, however fast the move looks.

itens: Look for the POC ahead, and factor it in
Earlier large stars help refine the target
Confirm the target fits before the next resistance
Don't move the target mid-trade without a reason from the plan
cenas.fala: The target has to be at least double the stop, but the guide also asks you to look at the path. Look for the POC ahead of your entry. If it sits on the path, factor it in, because the price may hesitate there. Earlier large stars help you refine the target, because they mark places where the move had already stalled. And confirm the target fits before the next resistance. If it doesn't fit, the risk-to-target relationship is worse than the plan assumed, and that's a reason to let the trade go. Finally, a rule of discipline: don't move the target mid-trade without a reason that comes from the plan. Moving a target out of hope is the shortest route to a confusing journal.
Chapter three: how to manage the trade when a reversal star appears.

itens: Long, and a red star appears: protect
Short, and a green star appears: protect
Protecting means moving the stop to the entry, or into profit
The star is a protection order, not an exit order
cenas.fala: This is the part of management worth memorising. If you're long and a red star appears, or you're short and a green star appears, the guide says to protect the trade. That can mean moving the stop to the entry, or into profit already. Notice the guide's wording: the star is a protection order, not an exit order. You're not closing the trade. You're taking risk off it, and letting the move continue if it continues. Many beginners close everything at the first warning, and miss the part of the move the target was waiting for. Protecting is a decision. Exiting is a different one, and you only take it when the plan calls for it.

Look at this example of a buy. The trade is running in your favour, and a red star appears on the path. It's a warning that the move may be losing strength. The guide's action is to protect: move the stop to the entry, or into profit. If the price keeps going, the trade stays protected. If the price turns, the protection is already in place, and the result is much closer to zero than it would otherwise have been. In every case, the decision was made before the star appeared. There was no panic, there was a plan.
Chapter four: when not to enter, and the time windows to avoid.

itens: Tangled averages, with signals alternating
A signal right below a resistance, with no room
Table showing different directions on the timeframes above
238 average or POC on the wrong side, with no room
A large star on the same candle as the signal
Outside the high-volume windows
cenas.fala: There are six situations where you should let it go. First: tangled averages, with signals alternating from one side to the other, which means a sideways market. Second: a signal right below a resistance, or above a support, with no room to the target. Third: the trend table shows different directions on the timeframes above. Fourth: the 238 average or the POC is on the wrong side, with no room. Fifth: a buy signal appears on the same candle as a large red star. The guide gives this case as an example of letting it go. Sixth: outside the high-volume windows, which we'll look at next. If any of these situations is on the chart, you don't have a trade.

itens: The hours are Lisbon time, in winter
Avoid 16:00 to 17:30
Avoid 20:45 to midnight, and 04:00 to 06:30
Check your clock: the hours shift with daylight saving
cenas.fala: The guide lists windows to avoid, outside the periods of highest volume. The hours are Lisbon time, in winter. Avoid four in the afternoon to half past five. Avoid quarter to nine at night until midnight. And avoid four to half past six in the morning. Always check your own clock, because the time difference between countries changes through the year, and a window read wrongly is a window used wrongly. Notice that this isn't a magic rule. It's a way of not trading during the moments when the movement tends to be slower or more irregular, and of being present when the system works best.

itens: Check the direction on the timeframes above
Check the background histogram and the 238 average
Check the POC and the corner: Good Volume or Low Volume
Check the time and the windows to avoid
Note each signal and what happened
cenas.fala: The routine before a session is short. First, you check the direction on the timeframes above, using the table. Second, you look at the background histogram and the 238 average, which tell you the context on each side. Third, you check the POC and the corner of the chart, to see whether there's Good Volume or Low Volume. Fourth, you confirm the time, and whether you're in one of the windows to avoid. And fifth, when signals appear, you note each one in the journal, with what happened. During the session, your job is to follow the process, and not react to every triangle. TrendShot gives you many signals. You don't need all of them.

cenas.titulo: What to record for each signal
itens: Time, timeframe and direction
The four confirmations, yes or no
If you entered: entry, stop, target and size
If a star appeared, and whether you protected the trade
Did you follow the plan? One sentence on what you learned
cenas.fala: The journal is what turns TrendShot into learning, and it matters even more in a minute-scale system. For each signal, record the time, the timeframe and the direction. Then the four confirmations, one by one, with yes or no. If you entered, record the entry, the stop, the target and the size you calculated. Also record whether a star appeared and whether you protected the trade. And finally, the most important question: did you follow the plan? After a few weeks, the journal shows you at which times and on which markets you're following the process, and where you're improvising. That's your map, and no video can replace it.

We've reached the end of the TrendShot Bootcamp. Remember the essentials: the crossover is the trigger, and the trend gives the direction. You only enter when the four confirmations are met, with the stop and the target at one to two and the size calculated. And when a reversal star appears, you protect, you don't close out of fear. Do the exercises, practise on a demo account, and write your journal from the very first signal. If you have questions, bring your cases to the community and to the live sessions at MoreThanMoney. I'm Ricardo Garcia. See you next time.
